html:
No. Not every tattoo can be covered up, and I would rather tell you that now than take your deposit and let you find out in the chair. Most tattoos can be covered, and I cover a lot of them, but there is a real group that cannot be covered well at the size you want, in the spot you want, with the design you want. That group is larger than people expect.

The phrase is the problem. "Cover-up" sounds like deleting, and it is not.

A cover-up is a design problem, not a delete button

The old ink stays in your skin. Nothing I do with a machine removes it. What I am doing is drawing a second tattoo over the first, bigger and darker and busier, and placing its solid blacks and deepest shadows exactly where the old ink sits, so your eye reads the new image and never goes hunting for what is underneath.

That is the whole craft of it. I am not hiding a tattoo, I am building a new one whose dark areas are shaped by somebody else's old lines. Every decision after that comes back to one question: can I put enough dark in the right places to win?

[[IMG:tattoo-crowned-skull-cover-up|Stencil over the old tattoo on the left, the finished crowned skull on the right. You can see how the dark areas were built to land on the old ink.]]

It is also why light, airy, fine line designs almost never work as cover-ups. A delicate flower in thin gray has nothing to fight with. If you want something soft and open, put it on clean skin.

The four things I check before I say yes

Every cover-up consultation I do runs through the same four checks, in this order. If one of them fails badly enough, I say no, and I say it before you pay a deposit.

1. How dark and how solid the old ink is

This is the first thing I look at and it decides the most. Faded, thin, ten-year-old linework gives me room to work and opens up a lot of design options. Heavy solid black, old tribal, a blackout patch or dense saturated color is a different animal, because I can only go darker than what is already there, and past a certain point there is no darker left.

Send me a clear daylight photo, no flash, no filter, straight on. Flash lies: it flattens old ink and makes it read lighter than it is, and then I quote you a design I cannot deliver.

What is on you nowHow it usually goes
Thin, faded linework, ten years or olderEasiest case. Wide range of subjects, and it does not always have to go much larger.
A name or script in thin blackUsually workable, as long as the new piece is a good deal bigger than the lettering.
Mid-tone gray shading, no hard blackWorkable. Realism and portrait subjects handle this well.
Solid black tribal or a blackout patchHard. The new design has to be built out of black and heavy shadow, or the old ink gets laser faded at a clinic first.
Dense saturated color over a wide areaHard. Expect laser, and expect the new piece to go considerably larger.
Hands, fingers, neck, feet, anything on the headHardest, no matter what the old ink looks like.

2. How big you will let the new piece go

A cover-up is almost always larger than the tattoo underneath, and how much larger is not up for debate, it is set by the old ink. As a working rule I want about twice the footprint of the original, and on heavy black I want more, because I need room outside the old shape to put light values. With no light areas there is no contrast, and with no contrast you get a dark smudge instead of an image.

People hear "twice the size" and get quiet. I understand it. You came in wanting the problem to get smaller and I am telling you it gets bigger. But a small cover-up over a dark tattoo is a job I will not do. It fails in daylight, it fails in photos, and you will be back in two years asking me to fix it, except now we are covering two tattoos instead of one.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-warrior-cover-up|A winged warrior woman in a crested helmet, built over old ink. The helmet, the wings and the shadow work give me somewhere to put the heavy black without the whole piece going flat.]]

The upside of going bigger is that you stop thinking of it as damage control. Sized properly, a cover-up is just a good tattoo, and the subjects that cover well are the ones I like doing anyway: Aztec and cultural work with heavy ornamental detail, roses and filler, skulls, and portraits with deep contrast. My post on cover-up ideas that actually hide old ink goes through the specific subjects and why they earn their keep.

3. Where it sits on your body

Placement decides how much room I have and how the piece holds up over the years. A forearm, an outer arm, a thigh, a calf, a shoulder or a back gives me space to expand into and skin that takes detail and keeps it.

Hands, fingers, the sides of the neck, the tops of the feet and anything on the head are a different conversation. There is no room to go bigger, those spots do not hold fine detail the same way, and old finger tattoos usually have ink spread underneath that the new design has to fight. I turn down more hand and finger cover-ups than any other kind, and it is not because I do not want the work. Ribs, stomach and the inner upper arm sit in the middle: they will take the work, but plan on more than one sitting.

4. Whether it needs laser fading first

Some cover-ups do not become possible until the old tattoo is knocked down first, and that is a laser clinic's job, not mine. I do not laser in the shop. I will tell you plainly when a piece needs it, refer you out, and design around whatever is left when you come back.

The clinic decides how many laser visits it takes and how far apart they go, so plan on the cover-up being months away rather than next week. Understand what you are buying, too. You are not paying to erase the tattoo, you are paying to knock it back far enough that I get my design options back. Partial fading is usually all I need for the design. Tell the clinic it is for a cover-up, and how far to take it is their call. I wrote a whole post on when I ask for laser fading and when I do not, because it is the thing people push back on hardest.

The jobs I turn down

These are the ones I refuse, consistently, and the reason is the same every time. I can already see the result and it is not something I will put my name on.

  • A small, light design over a solid dark tattoo. The physics do not work. You cannot put light over dark.
  • Light, open fine line or single needle work over anything. Nothing to fight with. It reads as two tattoos stacked.
  • Hand and finger cover-ups where the old ink is heavy. No room to expand and no way to win.
  • A cover-up with a hard deadline that is too close. Rushing one is how you end up with a bad one.
  • Somebody else's failed cover-up that is already maxed out on black. Sometimes the honest answer is laser before anyone tattoos you again, and how much is the clinic's call.
  • A reference the client will not let me change. If the design is locked and the design will not cover, we do not have a job. I need to move the shapes.
I would rather lose the booking than put my name on a cover-up that still reads as a cover-up.

Why hearing no is cheaper than a bad cover-up

Say I take a job I should have refused. You pay for the sitting at my rate of $150 an hour and walk out with something that looks acceptable that week. Then the new ink ages, loses a little density, and the old tattoo starts showing through underneath. Now you are looking at laser anyway, on two tattoos stacked instead of one, and then paying for a third tattoo, larger again, to cover both.

That is three bills instead of one, plus years of your life with something on your arm you do not want to explain. A no from me at the consultation costs you nothing. That is the entire argument.

A no is also rarely the end of it. Usually it means "not that design, not at that size, not in that spot," and there is a version that works. My job is to find it, tell you what it costs in money and in sittings, and let you decide. The finished ones are in the gallery, where the cover-ups are marked.

[[IMG:tattoo-catrina-woman-with-roses|A Catrina with roses. Ornamental detail like this gives me a lot of places to put a shadow, which is why these subjects cover so well.]]

What to send me before you book

Four things, and you will get a straight answer back.

  1. A clear photo of the existing tattoo, in daylight, no flash, shot straight on rather than at an angle.
  2. A rough measurement in inches. Hold a tape next to it if you can.
  3. What you would like to see there instead, with a reference image or two.
  4. Whether it has already been lasered, and roughly how many sittings you had.

Tell me up front how much bigger you are willing to go. That answer changes what I can offer you more than anything else on the list, and if it is "not much bigger," say so. I will tell you right away whether a design exists that fits inside it.

Most of my cover-ups end up in black and grey Chicano realism, because that style is built on deep contrast and ornamental detail, which is exactly what a cover-up needs. Check pricing and deposits so you know what you are walking into, then send the photo over. Quality takes time, excellence takes experience, and neither one comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.

title: Can Any Tattoo Be Covered Up? An Honest Answer

html:
Most cover-up ideas fail for the same reason. You picked the design because you like it, not because it can hold a dark shape. Those are two different questions, and only the second one decides whether the old tattoo disappears.

So this is how I sort cover-ups. Not by style, not by what looked good on somebody's mood board, but by how much old ink the design can swallow before it starts fighting for room. Get that part right and the rest is drawing.

A cover-up is a shadow, not a coat of paint

Tattoo ink is not paint and skin is not a canvas. The pigment sits down in the dermis, under the surface, and when I put new ink over old the two read together. Nothing gets erased. The old piece is still down there under the new one.

Which gives you the working principle for every cover-up I have ever done: the old tattoo has to become a shadow inside the new one. Every dark area in the existing piece needs a reason to be dark in the new design. An eye socket. The underside of a jaw. The deep side of a petal. A carved groove in stone. If I can give the old ink a job in the new picture, it stops reading as a mistake and starts reading as depth.

That also tells you, immediately, why light designs cannot do this work. There is no ink that lifts a dark one. White does not cover black. It sits in it and goes flat and gray, and now you have two problems instead of one.

[[IMG:tattoo-crowned-skull-cover-up|Same arm, before and after. On the left the new design is stenciled straight over the old dark tattoo. On the right the old ink is doing the shadow work inside the skull.]]

Cover-up designs ranked by how much old ink they swallow

Here is the sorting, plainly. The middle column is the honest answer about how much existing dark ink a design can take and still look like a finished piece, not a patch job.

Design typeOld ink it can absorbWhat actually does the hiding
Ornamental blackwork, mandala, filigreeAlmost anythingSolid black fields with pattern on top
Skull or skeletal workA lotSockets, nasal cavity, deep cast shadow
Big cat or heavy animal headA lotDark fur masses, open mouth, shadowed brow
Aztec stonework and relief carvingA lotCarved grooves read as pure black by design
Rose cluster with deep shadingA fair amountThe dark between petals, not the petals
Florals with heavy negative spaceModerate, and only if placed rightThe black behind the flowers, not the flowers
PortraitLimitedOnly the shadow side of the face. Faces need clean midtones
Script over scriptClose to noneNothing. Letters have gaps and the old letters live in them
Watercolor and soft color with no blackNoneNothing. There is no dark value anywhere in it
Fine lineNoneNothing. It is line with no mass
Anything the same size as the old pieceNoneNothing. Size is part of the coverage

What actually works

The designs that work all share one trait: large areas of the picture are supposed to be dark, and those areas can be moved around to land where the old ink is. That is the whole list. Style is secondary.

Skulls and skeletal work

A skull is the most useful shape in cover-up work because it is mostly holes. Eye sockets, nasal cavity, the shadow under the cheekbone and the jaw. Those want to be solid black anyway, so I can position the skull on your arm so the sockets land on the darkest part of the old tattoo. Nobody looks at a skull and thinks the eyes are too dark.

Add a crown, a hood, smoke, roses coming off it, and the piece grows in whatever direction it needs to grow to catch the corners of the old work.

Big cats and heavy animal heads

A tiger, a lion, a panther, a wolf. Same reason. An animal head in black and grey Chicano realism has dark fur masses, a shadowed brow, an open mouth that is pure black inside. That is a lot of usable darkness, and unlike a human face, an animal can carry heavy contrast without looking wrong. Push a portrait that dark and it stops looking like the person.

Aztec stonework

Stone relief is built out of shadow. The sun stone, eagle and jaguar carvings, carved serpents, stepped patterns. In real carved stone the grooves are dark because they are deep, so in the tattoo they are allowed to be flat black, and flat black is what hides old ink.

It is also a design language that tiles. If the old tattoo is an awkward shape, I can run the stonework out around it and the composition still makes sense, which is not true of a single centered subject. More of that style is on the Aztec and cultural work page.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-warrior-cover-up|Not stonework, but the same idea: a winged warrior woman in a crested helmet, built over an old red tattoo and a line-drawn heart. The dark feathers and the shading behind her do the hiding, not the fine detail.]]

Roses and florals, if the shading is real

Roses work, but not for the reason people think. It is not the petals that cover. It is the dark between the petals, the deep throat of the flower, and the leaves and background behind it. A rose drawn light and open covers nothing. A rose with real depth in it covers a lot.

Same with larger floral pieces. If the design is flowers floating on bare skin, it is decoration, not a cover-up. If the flowers sit on a dark ground, now we are working.

Ornamental blackwork and mandalas

This is the heaviest tool available and I do not reach for it first, because it is a commitment. Ornamental blackwork covers close to anything, since large parts of it are solid black by design and the pattern sits on top of that black. If a tattoo is too dark for a skull and fading is not on the table, ornamental is usually the answer that is left.

[[IMG:tattoo-rose-over-ornamental-mandala|Rose over an ornamental mandala, shown for the design rather than as a before and after. The dark ground behind the rose is the kind of area that does the covering in a cover-up.]]

What almost never works

These come up in nearly every cover-up conversation I have, and the answer is almost always no. Not because they are bad tattoos, but because none of them contain enough darkness to hide anything.

  • Fine line. Fine line is line and nothing else. There is no mass to it, so the old tattoo sits right there between the lines, fully visible. Fine line is for blank skin.
  • Script over script. People want to replace a name with a different word in the same spot. Letters have gaps and the old letters live in the gaps. Even in heavy blackletter you end up with ghost strokes running through your new lettering at every angle. If lettering has to go, it usually goes under a subject, not under more lettering.
  • Watercolor and soft color. A pure watercolor style deliberately leaves the black out. That is the entire look. There is nothing in the design to hide with.
  • Anything light and airy. Small birds, thin florals, single-needle ornamentals, open linework. Pretty, and useless here.
  • Anything the same size as what you have. This is the most common one. A cover-up the same footprint as the old piece has no room to put shadows anywhere except directly on top, and then the whole new tattoo is one dark blob.

If your heart is set on one of these, that is a real conversation to have. Sometimes the answer is laser first. Sometimes the answer is that the old piece gets covered with something heavy now, and you get the light piece you actually want somewhere else on your body. I would rather tell you that than take your money for something I know will disappoint you.

Size is part of the design, not a negotiation

Expect the new piece to be bigger than the old one, often twice the footprint, and more over heavy black. That is not upselling, it is geometry. The extra space is where the shadows go so they do not all pile onto the same square inch.

Placement matters as much as size. Sometimes the fix is not a bigger tattoo, it is a longer one. An old piece on the forearm that will not work as a standalone cover-up often works perfectly as one element inside a sleeve, because now I have the whole arm to compose across and the old ink becomes a dark passage in a much larger picture.

When I ask you to laser first

Sometimes the design you want is right and the only thing standing in the way is how dark the old tattoo is. That is when I send people for laser fading before we start.

Fading does not have to remove the old tattoo. It has to lighten it enough that your design choices open back up, so you are not locked into ornamental blackwork when what you wanted was a portrait or a piece with color in it. I go into when I ask for it and what it does to your calendar in the post on laser fading before a cover-up. How far the fading goes, and how many visits it takes, is the laser clinic's call, not mine.

What I need from you before I can answer any of this

One clear photo of the existing tattoo, taken in daylight, no flash. That is it, and I cannot give you a real answer without it. A photo tells me the size, the placement, how dark the ink actually is and how crisp the edges still are, and all four of those change what is possible.

Send that along with a rough measurement, what you would like to see there instead, and whether it has been lasered already. You will get a straight answer, including the answers people do not want to hear. If your idea will not cover what you have, I will say so before the needle, not after. For the longer version of that conversation, read my honest answer on whether any tattoo can be covered up.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.

You can see finished cover-ups alongside the rest of the work in the gallery, and the shop rate and deposit terms are laid out on the pricing and deposits page. When you are ready, send the photo and we will start booking a date.

title: Cover-Up Tattoo Ideas That Actually Hide Old Ink

html:
Sometimes I look at a photo of an old tattoo and tell somebody that what they want is not a cover-up problem yet. It is a fading problem first. That is not an upsell, because I do not do the fading. It is a drawing call, and it comes down to one thing: how many values I have to work with over that patch of skin.

Most of the cover-ups I do go straight over the original. A smaller share need the old piece lightened first. The broad version of that question is whether any tattoo can be covered up. This is the narrow one: when I ask for laser fading before a cover-up, what it buys the drawing, and what it does to your calendar.

What I mean by fading, and what I am not asking for

When I ask for fading, I am asking for the old tattoo to get lighter. I am not asking for it to be gone. Those are two different jobs.

For a cover-up I do not need the old piece erased. I need it quiet, far enough down that it stops dictating where my darks go. How many appointments that takes, and when to stop, is the laser clinic's call, not mine. Tell them you are fading for a cover-up, not removing it, and let them plan the treatment from there.

Mid-tones are the whole argument

A realistic tattoo is built out of mid-tones, not out of black. Black is only where a form ends. Everything that makes a face look like a face, or a rose look round, lives in the grays in between.

Picture a ladder of values running from bare skin at the top down to solid black at the bottom. On bare skin I have the whole ladder. Over a dark old tattoo the top half is gone, because anything I put there has to be at least as dark as what is already under it or the old piece reads through. My lightest usable value becomes somebody else's mid-tone. My mid-tones have to become black. The design goes flat in exactly the places I wanted depth.

Lighten the base a few steps and the ladder comes back. A mid-gray reads as a mid-gray again, and I can model the form. That is the entire reason I ask. It is not about hiding the old tattoo, because anybody can hide a tattoo under enough black. It is about having somewhere to go once it is hidden.

[[IMG:tattoo-crowned-skull-cover-up|The stencil sitting over the old piece on the left, finished on the right. Look at how much of that design exists to give the darks a reason to be there.]]

What a faded base changes for you

Three things: more designs on the table, a smaller possible piece, and fewer hours in my chair. In that order of importance.

More design options. Over an unfaded piece I steer you toward work that is naturally dark and busy: heavy black and grey Chicano realism, a warrior in full shadow, a skull, dense ornamental filler. Good tattoos, but they are the only tools on the bench. Over a faded base, portraits come back into play, and so do religious pieces that need open sky behind them.

A smaller piece. Unfaded cover-ups grow. They have to, because the design needs shapes big enough to swallow the old outline and somewhere else for the eye to go. Somebody wants a forearm piece, and the honest answer is that it has to run to the elbow. A faded base usually lets the design sit closer to the original footprint. Not the same size. Closer.

Fewer hours with me. Burying old ink means packing and layering over the same ground more than once. At $150 an hour that is real money. A lighter base means the darks need fewer passes. I would rather charge you for drawing than for burying.

What the design needsOver the old tattoo as it standsOver a faded base
Soft mid-tone shadingGone over the dark areas. Everything there becomes black.Available, and that is where depth comes from.
A face or a likenessRarely works. A likeness needs the full value range.Usually on the table.
Open skin, sky, negative spaceNo. Anything left open shows the old piece.Limited, but possible.
SizeHas to grow past the original footprint, often by a lot.Can sit closer to the original footprint.
ColorPushed dark and saturated so it does the hiding.Wider range. Lighter tones become usable.
Hours in the chairMore. Multiple passes to bury the old ink.Fewer. The darks go down in less time.
[[IMG:tattoo-jesus-portrait-with-thorns|A face like this needs the full range of values. Over a solid old tattoo I would not have them.]]

When I ask for it, and when I do not

I ask for fading when the old piece is dark, solid or hard-edged, or when the thing you want over it is delicate. I skip it when the old work is already light, or small, or when your design is going dark anyway.

I usually ask for fading when:

  • There is solid black fill, a blackout band or a heavy tribal outline underneath.
  • The lettering is bold and the letter shapes read through anything I put over them.
  • There is saturated color under a design you want in black and grey.
  • You want a face, a portrait, or anything where a likeness has to be right.
  • You want the new piece to stay roughly the size the old one is now.
  • The composition needs open skin: sky, clouds, water, room to breathe.

I usually do not bother when:

  • The old piece is years old, soft and already low contrast.
  • It is small enough that a bigger design absorbs it without effort.
  • Your design carries enough black on its own merit to cover it honestly.
[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-warrior-cover-up|Winged warrior over old work, no fading first. This design carries enough weight on its own that it did not need a lighter base.]]

How this works on the calendar

Plan in months, not weeks. Fading happens on somebody else's calendar, and I will not hold a tattoo date for you until we can both see what the base is going to look like.

  1. Send me a photo first. Daylight, no flash, the whole tattoo in frame, plus a rough measurement in inches. That costs nothing and it is the fastest way to find out whether fading is part of this at all.
  2. If I ask for fading, I point you somewhere. You book that on their calendar. Tell them the goal is a cover-up, not removal.
  3. Send me a new photo when they are done, or partway through. I design from the base in front of me, not from a picture taken last spring.
  4. Then we set a date and take a deposit. The deposit holds that date, and I set that date only after the clinic tells you the area is ready to be tattooed. How deposits work is on the pricing and deposits page.

If there is a date attached to this, a wedding or a summer where you want it visible, start the conversation about a year out. People come to me in March wanting a faded cover-up finished by June, and I cannot promise that, because the fading half of the timeline belongs to the clinic. More on timing in booking around summer and the gym.

I do not do the fading myself

I am a tattooer. I do not run a laser and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I refer that part out and then I do my half.

Do one thing properly and send people to somebody who does the other thing properly. When you come back, my job is to draw the piece the new base allows, which is almost always a stronger drawing than the one we would have settled for months earlier.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I'm not the artist for bargain hunters.

Start with the photo

Text a clear photo of the old tattoo to (708) 770-2754, or message me at @tat2nestuhh, and tell me what you want there instead. You will get a straight answer, including the ones people do not want: that it has to be bigger than you hoped, that it needs fading first, or that the idea you brought is too light to do the job. That conversation is cheaper before the needle than after it.

When you are ready, booking is here and the finished cover-ups are in the gallery. I am at 5920 W 111th St in Chicago Ridge, Monday through Saturday, 12pm to 7pm.

html:
Chicano black and grey is a tattoo style that came out of Mexican American Los Angeles: soft gray wash instead of packed color, a single needle instead of a heavy liner, and a set of images that carry real weight for the people wearing them. It is what I have built my work around, and it is what I get asked about more than anything else.

Most of what gets posted online as "Chicano style" is the imagery without the technique, or the technique with no idea what the imagery means. This is the long version: where it came from, what defines it on skin, what the main images carry, and what I watch people get wrong.

Where the Chicano tattoo style came from

It came out of Mexican American neighborhoods in Los Angeles and out of California prisons, and it reached tattoo shops in the 1970s. Nobody invented it in a studio. People invented it working with what they had.

The pachuco era

Pachuco culture emerged in the late 1930s in El Paso, Texas, and flourished among Chicano men in Los Angeles through the 1940s: zoot suits, ducktails, chains, and caló, the half English half Spanish slang. It faded in the 1960s, but the look and the attitude got handed down. Tattoos were part of it, usually small, on the hands and forearms, and usually put in by hand rather than by machine.

Guitar strings and tape player motors

Black and grey as a working method came out of California prisons, within Chicano and cholo culture from Los Angeles, before it ever reached a shop. Guitar strings got sharpened into needles. Cigarette ash and pen ink got thinned into a wash. Small motors pulled out of cassette players ran the machines. It was called jailhouse style, or joint style, before anybody called it black and grey.

Here is the part people skip: the limits created the look. With one needle and thinned pigment you cannot lay a bold outline and you cannot pack saturated color. What you can do is build tone, one light pass at a time, until a face appears. Every defining trait of the style traces back to that constraint.

Good Time Charlie's and the move into shops

Starting in the mid 1970s, the style crossed into professional shops and picked up the name black and grey. A shop called Good Time Charlie's Tattooland in East Los Angeles is where much of that crossing over happened. Charlie Cartwright, Jack Rudy and Freddy Negrete are the names attached to it, with Ed Hardy also credited for carrying it to a wider audience.

What changed was the equipment, not the thinking. Same one-needle approach, now with real machines and real pigment. That is the tradition I work in, and it is why I call my work black and grey Chicano realism rather than just realism.

What actually defines the style on skin

Four things: a single needle or a very tight grouping, gray wash built in layers, high contrast, and negative space doing as much work as the ink. There is no bold outline in the traditional American sense, and that absence is the reason the style reads differently from across a room.

  • Single needle and fine line. Thin line weight that varies inside one piece. A jawline might be a whisper and a hat brim a firm edge, in the same tattoo.
  • Gray wash. Black diluted to a range of values and laid down in passes. You are not filling an area, you are building it up until it reads as light falling on something.
  • High contrast. Deep blacks next to untouched skin. This work is dramatic on purpose. It is lit like a photograph with one hard light source, not like a flat illustration.
  • Negative space. Most of the white in these pieces is not white ink. It is skin I never touched. Deciding what to leave blank is most of the design work.
  • Composition over outline. With no containing black line, the piece holds together through value and shape alone. Get the composition wrong and no amount of shading rescues it.
ElementTraditional AmericanChicano black and grey
OutlineHeavy, uniform blackThin, varied, often absent
ColorBold and packed, limited paletteBlack thinned into gray values
ShadingSecondary to the lineThe entire point of the piece
Light sourceUsually implied or noneOne clear, hard light source
Bare skinGets filledLeft bare on purpose, it is the highlight
What carries it at 10 feetThe outlineThe contrast

One consequence: this style is slower. A design that takes three hours as bold traditional work takes longer in gray wash, because tone gets built in passes instead of dropped in once. That is not me stretching a session. That is the method.

[[IMG:tattoo-crying-woman-with-loyalty-script|Most of the light in her face is not ink at all. That is skin I left alone.]]

The iconography and what it carries

The images in this style are not decoration, and most of them are older than tattooing. If you are going to wear one for the rest of your life, you should know what it says.

Smile now, cry later

The two masks come from ancient Greek theater, where actors performed in masks and comedy and tragedy each had a face of their own. Thalia is the muse of comedy, Melpomene the muse of tragedy. The phrase attached to them in Chicano culture is also the title of a 1966 record by Sunny and the Sunliners on the Key-Loc label, a lowrider oldies standard.

It means discipline, not mood. You hold the feeling until you are somewhere you can let it out. People ask for it because it looks good on a forearm, which is fine, but I tell them what it says first.

[[IMG:tattoo-smile-now-cry-later-masks|The masks need room to breathe. Cramped, they turn into two blobs by year five.]]

La Catrina

José Guadalupe Posada made the original zinc etching around 1910 to 1912, and it was first published in 1913 in a satirical broadside. The name translates roughly to "the dapper female skull," and Posada's target was class pretension, people denying where they came from. Diego Rivera put her in his 1946 to 1947 mural "A Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park," dressed her in a Tehuana skirt and gave her a feathered serpent boa referencing Quetzalcoatl. That is where she stopped being a cartoon and became a national symbol.

When someone asks me for a "sugar skull girl," a Catrina is almost always what they mean. She makes a stronger piece once you know she started as a joke about pretending to be something you are not.

[[IMG:tattoo-catrina-woman-with-roses|A Catrina lives or dies on the bone structure under the makeup. Get the skull right and the flowers take care of themselves.]]

Our Lady of Guadalupe

The account is specific, and so is the image. In that account, she appeared to Juan Diego at Tepeyac Hill, in what is now northern Mexico City, between December 9 and 12 of 1531, and the image was left on his tilma, an Aztec cloak. That cloth hangs in the Basilica in Mexico City. Her feast day is December 12.

The elements are not optional: hands clasped in prayer, head tilted, eyes lowered, a pink tunic with a floral pattern, a blue-green mantle edged in gold and covered with eight-pointed stars, a black sash, a crescent moon beneath her feet, an angel with eagle wings holding her up, and a sunburst behind her.

If you bring me a reference where the mantle is the wrong color, the stars have been dropped, or the angel got cropped out to save room, I will say so. This is where I get particular about religious pieces. Do it right or pick a different subject.

Rosaries, clocks and roses

A rosary is a devotional object, not a necklace. Wrapped around a forearm or threaded through praying hands, the beads and the crucifix should be correct, not approximate. A clock almost always marks a specific moment, usually a birth or a death, so bring me the actual time and I will set the hands to it. Roses are the connective tissue of the whole style, which is exactly why a lazy rose ruins a good piece.

Lowriders and the street

Lowriding started in Southern California in the mid to late 1940s among Mexican American young people: low and slow, deliberately the opposite of the hot rod. California Vehicle Code section 24008 took effect January 1, 1958 and made it illegal to run a car modified to sit below the bottom of its wheel rims. In 1959 a mechanic named Ron Aguirre got around it with a hydraulic setup that let the driver raise the car on a switch. Whittier Boulevard in Los Angeles became the strip.

So a lowrider in a tattoo is not just a nice car. It is engineering that exists because somebody wrote a law against it. Honor that with correct body lines and a correct year, not a generic sedan.

Payasa and payaso

Clown makeup on a woman or a man. Same idea as the masks, moved off a prop and onto a face, which makes it harder to look away from. It also gives an artist a reason to push contrast, because painted skin next to bare skin is the kind of value jump this style feeds on.

Family portraits and lettering

Portraits are the anchor of Chicano black and grey. Grandmothers, children, people who have passed. The technique was built to do exactly this, which is why it suits portraits and memorials so well. If the person in the photo mattered to you, the reference photo matters more than the artist does.

Old English and script grew up alongside cholo graffiti and the placa, the calligraphic neighborhood lettering. It is a real discipline with real rules about weight and spacing, and it is the thing I see undersized more than anything else. Read sizing lettering for life before you commit to a name across a collarbone.

What people get wrong

Two kinds of errors, cultural and structural. Both are free to fix before the needle starts and impossible to fix after.

  1. The Aztec sun stone is not a calendar. Its name is the Piedra del Sol. It was dug up on December 17, 1790 at the Zócalo in Mexico City, carved between 1502 and 1520 under Moctezuma II, roughly 12 feet across and about 54,000 pounds of basalt. It uses calendar glyphs to talk about cycles of time, but it does not function as a calendar, and archaeologists read it as a ceremonial basin or altar. Wearing it is not the problem. Designing it without knowing what the four previous eras around the center face are is. That is what I work through before drawing Aztec and cultural work.
  2. Aztec is not Maya, and neither is Inca. Three separate civilizations, in some cases thousands of miles apart, in some cases centuries apart. Image boards mash them together constantly. Bring me a "Mayan warrior" that is actually an Aztec eagle warrior in Incan dress and I will untangle it with you.
  3. Copying somebody else's tattoo. Especially a memorial, or anything marking a specific affiliation. If it belongs to a person or a family, it is theirs. I will draw you something in the same tradition, never the same piece.
  4. Affiliation work. I do not put claims on people. Neighborhood markings, anything that labels you as belonging to something specific. I will tell you no, and I will tell you why.
  5. Sizing it like line work. Gradual tone needs physical room. A portrait squeezed into a panel that would suit a bold traditional rose has nowhere to put its mid-tones, and the mid-tones are the tattoo.
  6. Treating it as pure aesthetic. You do not have to be Mexican American to wear this style. You do have to know what you are wearing. That is the difference between honoring a tradition and decorating yourself with one.

How it holds up over the years

Gray wash ages well in one specific way and poorly in another, and the design has to account for both on day one. These pieces have no hard outline to blur outward, and a blurring outline is what gives heavily lined work its fuzzy border. What they do lose is contrast, and contrast is the entire style.

So I leave more bare skin than looks right when you first see the stencil. A piece packed edge to edge with mid gray looks rich for a year, then closes up into one flat value. A piece with real separation between the darks and the untouched skin has room to lose some contrast and still read. For the full comparison I wrote about black and grey versus color separately.

How I build a Chicano piece, and what to bring me

Bring reference and bring specifics: the actual photo, the actual time on the clock, the actual date, and a clear idea of placement. I draw custom for this style every time, because a Catrina designed for a calf and a Catrina designed for a forearm are two different drawings.

I will also tell you the truth about size. If your idea needs eight inches and you want it in four, I will say so before you have paid anything, because I would rather lose the booking than put out a piece that turns to mush in five years. Look through the gallery and see what a given amount of room actually buys you.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I'm not the artist for bargain hunters.

My rate is $150 an hour for large and ongoing work, small pieces are quoted flat, and a deposit holds the date. I am at 5920 W 111th St in Chicago Ridge, Monday through Saturday, 12pm to 7pm, closed Sunday. Everyone getting tattooed is 18 and over, no exceptions, and Illinois law does not allow a parent to consent on your behalf. If you have a Chicano piece in mind and you want it done properly, start here or call the shop at (708) 770-2754.

Don't be average. Be set apart.

html:
The religious tattoo ideas I get asked for are the same handful every year: the Virgin of Guadalupe, a Christ portrait with the crown of thorns, praying hands wrapped in a rosary, a cross or a crucifix, cherubs and archangels, and a line of scripture. Each carries something specific, and most get asked for at half the size they need.

The shop is called Anointed Ink for a reason, and a lot of what comes through the door is faith-led. I am not going to preach at you. What I can tell you is what each image traditionally carries, where the design goes wrong, and what it takes to hold up on skin over the years. Finished work is on the religious pieces page.

The short version

The size column is my own working minimum, not a rule anyone handed me. It is where I have watched these pieces stay readable instead of closing up.

ImageryWhat it traditionally carriesHow big I will do it
Guadalupe, full figureProtection, home, Mexican Catholic identity9 inches minimum, forearm length or more
Virgin MaryIntercession, grief carried well, motherhood6 inches for the face to read
Christ with thornsSacrifice, the Passion7 inches, usually a shoulder or half sleeve
Praying hands and rosaryDevotion, a prayer you actually keep6 inches for the hands, plus the bead run
Plain crossFaith, stated plainlyOne of the few that works small, 2 to 3 inches
Crucifix with the bodyThe cost of it, not just the symbol5 inches or the figure closes up
CherubInnocence, watchfulness, often a child5 inches for the face
Archangel MichaelProtection with a sword in it8 inches and up. Wings need room
Scripture in scriptThe line you live bySized by letter height, never phrase length

Guadalupe and the Virgin Mary are not the same request

People use the two names interchangeably and they are different pieces. Guadalupe is a fixed composition. Mary is an open one.

Guadalupe is the image tied to the 1531 apparition at Tepeyac, in what is now northern Mexico City. The composition almost never changes: she stands on a crescent moon, an angel holds her up at the base, rays surround her, her mantle is star-covered, her hands together, her eyes lowered. Because everyone knows the image, everyone notices when you change it. Cut the rays short and you are editing something people know by heart. That tie to heritage is why she so often shares an arm with Aztec and cultural work.

Mary on her own gives you more room. Veiled head, hands in prayer, sometimes a rosary in the fingers, sometimes a single tear. She reads as intercession, and as grief being carried rather than hidden. I tattoo her more for people who lost their mother than for any other reason.

[[IMG:tattoo-virgin-mary-praying|Mary with the rosary. Almost all of this piece is fabric, and fabric is where a Marian tattoo is won or lost.]]

The craft note nobody expects: a Marian piece is mostly cloth. The face is maybe fifteen percent of the work. The rest is folds, and folds are built from value, not line. Flat drape and the whole thing reads like a sticker no matter how good the face is.

Christ portraits and the crown of thorns

A Christ portrait is a portrait first and a religious piece second. If the face does not read as a face, no amount of meaning saves it.

The crown of thorns comes from the Passion accounts, where soldiers plait thorns into a crown (Matthew 27, Mark 15, John 19). On skin it does two jobs. It carries the meaning, and it hands me a hard graphic edge to set against the soft gray wash of the face. Thorns are crisp, the face is smooth, and the eye reads both because they are not competing.

[[IMG:tattoo-jesus-portrait-with-thorns|Thorns give me a hard edge to run against soft gray wash. That contrast does more work than people realize.]]

Everything true of portraits is doubled here, because you are not bringing me a photograph. You are bringing a painting somebody already stylized. If the reference is muddy, low contrast, or three images stitched together, you will hear it before we start. My post on picking the reference photo covers what I need to see.

Praying hands, rosaries, crosses and crucifixes

These get grouped because they are usually the same tattoo. Hands, beads, a crucifix at the end of the chain.

The praying hands reference nearly everybody brings traces back to one drawing: Albrecht Durer's 1508 study of an apostle's hands. That is why the pose looks familiar to people who have never seen the original. Hands are as demanding as faces. Knuckles, tendons, the shape of the nails, the gap where the palms do not quite meet. Bad hands read as bad hands immediately, in a way a slightly off face somehow does not.

On rosaries, count the beads. A standard rosary is five decades of ten, a single bead between decades, a centerpiece, then a pendant of five beads (one, then three, then one) down to the crucifix. People who pray it will count what is on your arm, and I have had a client clock a bad count from across the room. If we wrap the chain around a forearm, we decide up front where the crucifix lands, because that is the anchor of the composition.

Cross or crucifix is a real distinction. A cross is the bare form. A crucifix carries the body on it. I will not argue you into either, but pick on purpose. A plain cross is one of the few religious pieces that works at two or three inches. A crucifix is not. Put a full figure on a three-inch cross and in fifteen years it is a smudge with arms.

Cherubs and archangels carry different weight

Cherubs and archangels are not the same thing, and the difference is worth knowing before it is on you permanently.

The winged infant everyone means by "cherub" comes out of Renaissance and Baroque painting. The two leaning on the ledge at the bottom of Raphael's Sistine Madonna, 1512, are the pair the whole world copied. Scripture's cherubim are something else: guardians posted at Eden beside a flaming sword in Genesis 3, and the four-faced beings beneath the throne in Ezekiel. So when you ask me for a cherub, you mean the painting, not the text. Just know which one you are wearing. Cherubs also come to me constantly as memorials for a child, and when that is the reason, say so, because it changes how I build the face.

Archangels are a different mood. Most people who ask want Michael, usually for the same reason: Revelation 12 puts him at the head of the war in heaven against the dragon. Sword raised, often standing over a serpent. He is the one people get after something they had to survive. Gabriel is the messenger of the Annunciation in Luke 1, and in religious art he carries a lily or a horn instead of a blade.

[[IMG:tattoo-archangel-with-sword|Michael with the sword raised. Wings and a blade both want length, which is why these land on forearms and shoulder blades.]]

Wings eat space and swords want a long run, which pushes archangels onto forearms, shoulder blades and calves. Squeeze one into a four-inch square and the wings become texture instead of wings. The Michael above is in the gallery with the rest of the religious work.

Scripture: pick the line before you pick the font

The verse and the lettering are two separate decisions and people collapse them into one. Choose the words first, then we size the letters, then we find the spot that fits those letters.

Most requested: Psalm 23, Psalm 91, Proverbs 3:5-6, Philippians 4:13, Isaiah 41:10, Joshua 1:9. The trouble is almost never the verse, it is the length. Someone wants four sentences of Psalm 91 on the inside of a wrist, and there is no version of that still legible in ten years, because ink spreads a little as the years go by and the gaps inside the letters close first.

Two ways out. Cut to the clause that actually matters to you, or tattoo the chapter and verse reference instead of the text. The reference is short, ages cleanly, and quietly requires you to know the passage. My post on sizing script for life has the letter-height math.

A face in gray wash and script beside it are two different tattoos

This is the technical heart of the category, and it is why religious pieces go wrong more often than anything else I do. A portrait and a line of lettering are built by opposite methods, so setting them next to each other is a composition problem, not a decoration problem.

A face is built from value. Soft edges, no hard outline, gray wash packed in layers and worked until the gradient is smooth. What makes it read from six feet is the range between the darkest dark and open skin. Detail only makes it read from six inches.

Script is the opposite. It is built from line weight and negative space, and the gaps between and inside the letters are the actual design. Every one of those gaps narrows over the years, so script gets sized for what it looks like decades out, not for the day I finish it.

Set them side by side and if the lettering sits too close, the soft edge of the face and the spread from the letters meet in the middle and both lose. So I leave deliberate open skin between a face and its script. Clients ask me to fill that gap almost every time. I do not. That space is load-bearing. Same reason my black and grey Chicano realism treats open skin as a design element instead of unfinished area.

Go bigger than you first want to

Nearly every religious piece I book gets asked for at roughly half the size it needs. I am not upselling you. I am telling you what fits.

Count the elements in a Guadalupe: a face, two hands, a star-covered mantle, the folds under it, a border of rays all the way around, an angel at the base, a crescent moon. Seven subjects. At five inches the stars turn into dots, the angel turns into a shape, the folds disappear. At ten inches each element gets to be itself. Same design, completely different tattoo.

Then add time. Every line ends up slightly wider than the day it went in. A design already ninety percent covered at four inches has nowhere to put that. At nine inches it has room to age into. Placement follows the composition, not the reverse: a forearm suits a rosary run or an archangel on the diagonal, a shoulder suits a portrait with a thorn crown. Tell me the image and I will tell you where it goes.

How to bring me an idea

Bring the reference, not the description. "A Jesus piece" tells me nothing. An actual image, a photo of the spot, and anything already tattooed nearby tells me everything.

Tell me what it is for. A cherub for a child you lost gets built differently than a cherub you like the look of. The rate is $150 an hour for larger work (small pieces are quoted flat), a deposit holds the date, and you can start at booking.

And I will tell you when your idea will not work. Psalm 91 in full on a wrist, or a crucifix at two inches, you will hear it before a stencil goes on. Losing a booking bothers me less than putting my name on a piece that falls apart.

Don't be average. Be set apart.

html:
People say "I want an Aztec tattoo," and that could mean six completely different pieces. Before we talk placement or price I need to know which symbol you want and what you believe it means, because a good half of what people have been told is wrong.

Here is the straight version: what these symbols carry, where the reference actually comes from, and what makes each one work or fail on skin. I do a lot of Aztec and cultural work, and the failed pieces I get asked to fix did not fail on shading. They failed on geometry and research.

The six pieces people actually ask me for

Nearly every request lands in one of six places.

SymbolWhat it is understood to carryWhat the design demands
The Sun Stone (the so-called Aztec calendar)The world-ages and the cycling of time. Not a working calendar.Flat real estate and rings that are genuinely true
Eagle warrior (cuāuhtli)Rank you had to earn, courage, the sunCorrect helmet structure and counted feathers
Jaguar warrior (ocēlōtl)The other elite order, paired with the eaglePelt texture, which eats hours
Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpentWind, Venus, learning, the priesthoodA limb it can wrap, not a flat square
Huitzilopochtli and the hummingbirdPatron of the Mexica, and the fallenSmall and simplified, or large. No middle
Popocatépetl and IztaccíhuatlDevotion, grief, loyalty past deathTwo figures and a landscape. Back, chest or full outer arm

The Sun Stone is not a calendar

The carving everyone calls the Aztec calendar does not tell time. It uses calendar glyphs to talk about cycles of time, which is a different job, and you can no more read today's date off it than off a painting of a clock.

The real object is basalt, about 12 feet across, weighing about 24,600 kilograms. It carries the name glyph of Moctezuma II, putting the carving in the early 1500s, and it came out of the Zócalo in Mexico City on December 17, 1790 during work around the cathedral. The face in the middle is still argued over: Tonatiuh the sun, Tlaltecuhtli the earth, or a night-lord figure, depending which scholar you read. The four panels boxed around it are four previous world-ages, named Four Jaguar, Four Wind, Four Rain and Four Water. Around those runs the ring of twenty day signs, and the outer band is two fire serpents, xiuhcoatl, with human heads coming out of their mouths. Near the top sits the date 13 Reed, which lines up with 1479.

That should change the ask. If you wanted a calendar, you want something else. If you wanted creation and destruction on a loop, you are in the right place.

It also sets the craft problem. The stone is built on concentric rings: every ring a true circle sharing one center, the twenty day signs evenly divided. People measure that with their eyes without knowing they are doing it, because this carving is on restaurant walls and posters and album covers. If your rings wobble, or one drifts off center, or the day signs crowd on one side and stretch on the other, it reads crooked to everybody and nobody can say why. So I draw it on center lines and check the divisions before anything starts, and I push it toward flat ground: upper back, chest, outer shoulder blade, the flat of the thigh. On a round forearm a true circle photographs as an ellipse from every angle but one.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-sun-stone-medallion|Sun stone work. If the rings are not true and concentric, the whole piece reads crooked and nobody can tell you why.]]

The eagle and the jaguar were ranks, not costumes

Eagle warriors (cuāuhtli) and jaguar warriors (ocēlōtl) were the two elite orders of the Aztec military, and nobody was born into them. Boys started formal training around 17, took adult standing by capturing their first prisoner alive, and reached these orders only after roughly four captives or a genuinely notable deed. The origin is worth knowing before you wear one: two gods, Nanahuatzin and Tecuciztecatl, threw themselves into a fire and rose as the sun and the moon, and an eagle and a jaguar went into the fire right behind them and came out singed. That is where the Nahuatl name for a brave warrior, eagle-jaguar, comes from. The archaeology is real too. The House of the Eagles at the Templo Mayor held life-size warrior figures, and the rock-cut temple at Malinalco has eagles and a jaguar carved out of bedrock.

Here is the detail that separates a warrior piece that lands from one that does not. The eagle helmet is an eagle's head with the beak held open, and the man's face looks out from inside that open beak. It is not a bird mask sitting flat on a face. Plenty of the reference floating around social media gets this wrong, and once you see it correctly you cannot unsee the wrong version. The same goes for feathers, which have a count and a direction and a repeating spacing. Guessed feathers fan out evenly like a duster and the headdress loses all its weight. Most of this belongs in black and grey Chicano realism, and I broke the style down in the Chicano style guide.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-warrior-bear|Feathered headdress. Feathers need a spacing rule and a direction, or the whole headdress goes soft.]]

Quetzalcoatl is older than the Aztecs

Quetzalcoatl is not an Aztec invention, and the gap is not small. The name is quetzalli, the plumage of the quetzal bird, plus coatl, serpent: a serpent of precious feathers. He was already worshipped at Teotihuacan by around the first century, spread across Mesoamerica through the Late Classic period from roughly 600 to 900, and appears in Maya form as Kukulkan and Q'uq'umatz. The earliest known image is on a stela at the Olmec site of La Venta, around 900 BC. So calling it an Aztec symbol runs about two thousand years short. That does not make it a wrong tattoo, it makes it a bigger one than you thought.

He is tied to wind, Venus, the sun, merchants, the arts and knowledge, and he was patron of the priesthood. In his wind form, Ehecatl, he wears a cut conch shell on his chest as a wind jewel: a specific object with a specific shape, worth getting right if that is the aspect you want.

A serpent wants to wrap, and that is the whole design note. He belongs on a sleeve, a calf or the ribs, where the body provides the spiral and the piece changes as you turn. Boxed into a flat rectangle on a shoulder blade, a feathered serpent becomes a decal. Give the head room, because the head carries most of the detail.

Huitzilopochtli, and why the hummingbird

Huitzilopochtli's name is literally a hummingbird. It comes from huītzilin, hummingbird, and ōpōchtli, the left hand side, giving "hummingbird of the south" or "left-handed hummingbird," because Aztec cosmology put the south on the left. He was patron god of the Mexica and a solar and war deity, and his red shrine stood atop the Templo Mayor beside Tlaloc's blue one. In the Coatepec story, Coatlicue conceives from a ball of feathers, her existing children take offense, and he comes out fully armed, kills his sister Coyolxauhqui and scatters his four hundred brothers across the sky.

The part that matters for tattoos is in the Florentine Codex: warriors who died in battle went to the house of the sun, and after four years there they came back as hummingbirds and butterflies. That is why a hummingbird next to a sun stone is not decoration. It is a specific idea about what happens to people who died hard, and it crosses into memorials more than anything else in the Aztec vocabulary. If you are getting one for somebody, tell me who they were and how you lost them. It changes the drawing, and I would rather know.

Practical note: every failed hummingbird I have been shown was asked to hold wing detail it had no room for. Under about three inches we simplify the wings on purpose, because a simplified small bird is usually a piece you still like in ten years and a crowded one usually is not.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-sun-stone-hummingbird|Hummingbird with the sun stone. For most of the people who ask me for this, it is a memorial.]]

The warrior and the princess: an old story and a 1940 painting

The legend is old. The picture on your phone is from 1940, and knowing that makes your tattoo stronger, not worse.

Iztaccíhuatl means "white woman" in Nahuatl and is nicknamed La Mujer Dormida, the Sleeping Woman, because the four snow-capped peaks read as the head, chest, knees and feet of a woman lying on her back when you view the range from east or west. Popocatépetl means smoking mountain, and it still smokes. In the Tlaxcaltecan telling she was a princess and he a warrior sent to fight in Oaxaca with her hand promised on his return. A lie reached her that he had fallen in battle, and she died of the grief. When he came home he carried her body out and knelt beside it, and the gods buried the two of them in snow and made them into the mountains.

Now the image everybody actually brings me: warrior in a feathered headdress kneeling over a woman in white on a mountaintop, smoke behind them. That composition is a painting, La Leyenda de los Volcanes, made in 1940 by Jesús Helguera, a Mexican painter who lived from 1910 to 1971. A tobacco company, Cigarrera la Moderna, commissioned him to paint for its calendars, Imprenta Galas de México printed them, and they ended up hanging in homes and shops all over Mexico. That is how the image got everywhere. Nearly every Popo and Izta tattoo I have been handed is a Helguera, whether the person holding it knows the name or not. I do not say that to talk anyone out of it. I say it because once you know you are working from a romantic Mexican painting and not from a codex, you stop straining to make it look ancient and render it as what it is, and the read comes out clearer.

Size is the hard conversation. Two full figures, a landscape and a sky is not a small tattoo. To stay legible years from now it needs a full back, a chest panel, or the entire outer arm. I have turned this down at five inches on a forearm more than once. At that scale the two faces are a few needle widths across, and no technique keeps them looking like faces.

What separates Aztec work that reads right

Geometry and reference, not shading ability. Every artist I respect can render a face. Fewer will stop and measure.

  • Rings true, concentric, evenly divided. Anyone who has seen the original catches a wobble instantly.
  • Feathers get a spacing rule. Count them, space them, taper them, point them.
  • A headdress sits on a skull. If the band does not wrap the head in correct perspective, the face underneath goes flat no matter how well it is rendered.
  • Bring the original reference, not a tattoo of a tattoo. Three generations of copying and the glyphs stop being glyphs and start being decoration shaped like glyphs.
  • Glyphs are writing. A day sign has a correct form. If you want a specific date sign or name glyph, we look it up together instead of improvising it.

Most of this I do in black and grey, because stone is gray and the texture work carries it. Feathers are the exception worth arguing about, and I went through that choice in black and grey versus color.

Bring me the reason, not just the picture

For a lot of the people in my chair these are heritage pieces, and I treat them that way. Somebody's grandmother grew up in Puebla and could see those two volcanoes from the roof. Somebody's father wore a sun stone on his forearm for thirty years. That context changes how I draw it, and it is the difference between a tattoo of a symbol and a tattoo that carries something.

So when you message me, give me three things: which symbol, why that one, and where it is going. A rough size in inches helps, photos of your actual reference help more, and finished work is in the gallery.

My rate is $150 an hour and a deposit holds the date, with the breakdown on pricing and deposits. Be realistic: a sun stone at a size that stays readable is usually multiple sessions, and a Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl back piece is measured in sittings, not hours. Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither one comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.

If that is the piece you want done right, book a date and bring your reference. Don't be average. Be set apart.

title: Aztec Tattoo Meanings and How to Design One Well

html:
Script tattoo lettering fails for one reason more than all the others combined: it was ordered too small. Ink does not stay exactly where the needle put it. Over the years it settles and spreads a little under the skin, so thin strokes thicken and the gaps inside the letters close up. A word you read on my stencil becomes a smudge you squint at from three feet. I have been tattooing over 25 years, and lettering is still the work I turn down most.

Why small lettering closes up

Letters do not need bad line work to blur. They blur because every line gains a little width over time, and small letters have no spare white to give away. Two things go first: the thin strokes, which have nothing in reserve, and the counters.

Counters are the typographer's word for the white enclosed inside a letter: the hole in an "o", the eye of an "e", the loop of a "g". Your eye reads a word by its counters as much as by its outline. Fill them in and the word becomes a shape.

Think in ratios, not sizes. Say a line gains half a millimeter on each side over two decades, and that figure is my estimate, not a measurement. A letter with a 4mm counter still has 3mm of open white and you would never notice. A letter with a 1mm counter is shut. So the question is never how small you can go. It is how much white sits between your strokes, and how much of it you can afford to lose.

Old English, Chicano fine line, and modern calligraphy

These three are not interchangeable and they do not fail the same way. Old English dies in the counters, Chicano fine line dies in the strokes, and modern calligraphy dies in the thins.

Old English (blackletter)

Old English is the tattoo name for blackletter, the heavy upright hand European scribes used before printing. Fat vertical stems, sharp diagonal cuts, almost no white inside the letter. The stems are the most durable thing in lettering because they start out wide. The counters are the least durable: on a proper blackletter "e" the white inside is a sliver. It is also the hardest of the three to read in a long line. Names, single words, years, a short phrase. Not a sentence.

[[IMG:tattoo-blackletter-year-2001|A year in blackletter. Four characters, cut big on purpose so the white inside the zeros has room to give as the ink settles.]]

Chicano fine line script

Fine line script is the signature hand of the style and the most fragile thing I put on skin. It came out of Southern California in the 1970s, when single-needle work and thinned-down black that had been done in prisons moved into professional shops in East Los Angeles, at Good Time Charlie's Tattooland, with Charlie Cartwright, Jack Rudy and Freddy Negrete. Same lineage that gives us black and grey Chicano realism. A one-needle line has nothing in reserve, so fine line needs real height and the most honest conversation about word count.

Modern calligraphy and brush script

Heavy downstrokes, hair-thin upstrokes, and the contrast is the whole look. Lose the thins and it stops being calligraphy and turns into wobbly cursive. It holds up longer than fine line and not as long as blackletter.

StyleWhat goes firstMy minimumWhere it holds
Old English / blacklettercounters close3/4 inch (19mm) cap heightforearm, chest, upper back, outer arm
Chicano fine line scriptstrokes thicken and merge1/2 inch (13mm) lowercase body, 1 inch capsforearm, chest, thigh, upper back
Modern calligraphy / brushthin upstrokes fill in5/8 inch (16mm) lowercase bodyforearm, collarbone, thigh

Those are my figures, for my hand. Another artist will give you different ones. What does not change is the trade: more letters means smaller letters means a shorter readable life.

Spacing is half the job

Height gets all the attention and spacing decides whether the word survives. Two letters set too close merge into one dark mass long before either letter softens on its own.

  • Between letters. One stroke width of open skin at minimum, more when the strokes are thin. Two stems closer than their own width will find each other.
  • Between words. A full letter width. In a long quote, tight word spacing kills readability at distance before the letters do.
  • Between lines. The tails of the top line (g, y, p) cannot touch the stems of the next (l, h, k). Tangled lines age into a hedge.
  • Connections in script. Letters join with a deliberate curve, not a spot where two strokes happen to touch. A touching joint becomes a blot.

This is why I push back on word count. "Only God Can Judge Me" is seventeen letters plus spaces. At a size that lasts, that is two lines filling an inner forearm. Cut it to three words or give it the room.

Where lettering holds and where it does not

Flat, stable skin holds lettering: forearm, chest, upper back, outer bicep, thigh. Skin that folds, stretches or works hard all day does not: fingers, the inner wrist, feet, and long horizontal text across the ribs or stomach.

The forearm is my first choice for a full line of text. Flat, stable, and you can read it yourself. Across the collarbones works for a name if the letters are big. Upper back, outer arm and the front of the thigh all take size, and size is what lettering wants.

Fingers are the hardest surface on the body for lettering. Your hands work every waking hour and the sides of your fingers press together all day. I will do them, and before you sit down I will tell you the work is not going to stay crisp and will want touch-ups. That is the location, not the work. The inner wrist is small, thin-skinned, and exactly where people want the tiniest script, which is the request I turn down most. Ribs and stomach move constantly, so keep text there short and scale it up.

[[IMG:tattoo-crying-woman-with-loyalty-script|One word, cut big, built into the piece instead of squeezed in beside it. That is how script is supposed to live inside a design.]]

Most of my lettering is not standalone anyway: a banner in a memorial, a name under a portrait, a verse worked into a religious piece. Text next to heavy shading has to be cut larger still, and I leave a margin of untouched skin around a banner on purpose. It looks like wasted space at the appointment and it is what gives the lettering room to stay readable later.

Why freehand lettering is unforgiving

I stencil most lettering and freehand it only when the body demands a curve a flat stencil cannot make. Lettering is the least forgiving thing there is to freehand, because a letter has no tolerance. A face can absorb a stroke that lands a millimeter off its mark. An "R" cannot.

A stencil printed flat and wrapped around a round bicep fights you: the ends pull in, the middle bows, the baseline wanders. So for script that wraps an arm or rides a collarbone, I draw it on with a marker. Then you stand up, we check it in the mirror with your arm hanging the way it actually hangs, and I redraw. That is part of the appointment, not wasted time. What I will not do is needle a freehand quote with no marker stage first.

Check the spelling twice, then check it again

I do not start until you have read the stencil out loud, letter by letter, and told me it is right. Misspelled tattoos do not happen because nobody checked. They happen because everybody assumed somebody else did.

  • The exact text, typed out. Something I can copy and paste, in the capitalization you want. Not a screenshot, not handwriting, not "you know the one".
  • Names spelled from a document. A birth record, an ID, a headstone. Not from memory. People misspell family names they have said out loud their whole lives.
  • A decided date format. 03.14.2009, March 14 2009, and MMIX are three different tattoos. I check Roman numerals twice because they are the easiest thing here to get wrong.
  • Another language confirmed by a person. If it is not English, I need it confirmed by somebody who reads and writes it, not by a translation app. Accents change meaning: "papá" and "papa" are not the same word. Hebrew and Arabic read right to left and get mangled when the text is copied wrong.

If you cannot get the text confirmed I will move the appointment rather than guess. I would rather lose the booking than put a permanent typo on you.

What it costs and how to start

My rate is $150 an hour for large and ongoing work, small pieces get a flat quote, and a deposit holds the date. Lettering looks simple, and that does not make it cheap. An even, correctly spaced, correctly sized line is where twenty-five years shows up, and it is the part nobody notices until it is missing.

[[IMG:tattoo-hourglass-and-est-lettering|An "Est." date built into the design rather than tucked underneath it, sized to give it room to hold its shape.]]

Message me the exact text, where you want it, and whether it should read to you or to the person standing in front of you. I will tell you what size it needs, and if that size does not fit the spot you picked, I will tell you that too. See finished work in the gallery, read pricing and deposits first, and book your date when you are ready. For the style this lettering belongs to, start with Chicano black and grey tattoos, and for timing, read how to book a tattoo with me.

Don't be average. Be set apart. That goes for the words you put on yourself, too.
