title: Old English and Script Tattoos: Sizing for Life

html:
The reference photo is the one decision that settles how a portrait turns out. A portrait can only hold the detail that is already in the photograph, so by the time you hand me the image, most of the result is already decided. I am not inventing a face. I am reading one and carrying it across to skin.

I send back a lot of reference photos, and people sometimes take that personally. It is not personal. It is me refusing to take $150 an hour for a piece that is never going to look like the person you love.

The photo is your budget of detail

Think of the photograph as a budget, because every step after it spends some of that budget and no step adds any back. The camera already lost something the day the picture was taken. My drawing loses a little when I simplify what the lens saw. The machine loses a little more putting it into skin instead of onto paper. Then time takes its cut, because ink spreads a small amount under the skin over the years, and the tightest detail in the piece is the first thing to close up.

So I want to start with more information than the tattoo needs, not exactly enough. A photo that looks fine at thumbnail size on your phone is usually the thinnest possible budget. When the budget runs out mid-piece, I have to invent, and invented detail is where likeness dies. Nobody can tell you why the tattoo looks wrong. They just know it is not him.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.

Light does more for a portrait than anything else

I need light coming from one clear direction. Black and grey Chicano realism is built out of values, not outlines, so the shape of a face comes entirely from where the light stops and the shadow starts. Give me a photo with a lit side and a shadow side and I can build a skull under that skin. Give me a flat photo and I am rendering a mask.

The two lighting situations that cost me the most are direct flash and backlight. Flash fired straight at someone flattens everything and burns the forehead, the nose and the cheekbone to blank white, and there is no information in blank white. Backlight does the opposite and turns the face into a dark shape with a bright rim. Both are photos of a person. Neither is a photo of a face.

What I want is window light. Put someone a few feet from a window, turn them slightly toward it, no flash, and you get one direction of light with detail surviving on both the bright side and the shadow side.

[[IMG:tattoo-classical-statue-portrait|A statue is simple to photograph because the light does the work. A face needs the same thing: one direction, a light side, a shadow side.]]

Contrast is the other half of it, and here is the part most people have never considered: your skin is the brightest value in the tattoo. I cannot add light. White ink does not stay bright in my experience, so I do not build a face on it. That means if your skin tone is deeper, the reference needs more separation between its values, not less, because I have less room to work in. A washed out gray photo becomes a washed out gray tattoo. Color realism has its own version of this problem, since kitchen light and phone auto-color make skin tones lie. If you are still deciding between the two, I went through it in black and grey vs color.

Focus and resolution: the eye test

Open the photo on the biggest screen you have and zoom all the way in on one eye. If the lashes, the edge of the iris and the wet line of the lower lid stay crisp, the photo can carry a portrait. If they turn to mush or break into little square blocks, it cannot, and nothing I do anywhere else on the face will make up for it.

Eyes are where recognition lives, with the corners of the mouth second. Everything else is supporting cast. A portrait with soft eyes and beautifully rendered hair still gets the same reaction from family, which is a long pause and then a polite sentence.

Two things fool people about resolution. First, a large file with a small face in it is still a small face. A twelve megapixel group shot where your grandmother's head is the size of a fingernail has almost nothing in it. What counts is how many pixels sit across the face, not how big the file is. Second, phone portrait mode. That depth effect often softens the hairline, the ears and the edge of the shoulders, and the hairline is exactly where a face meets the rest of the head.

Straight on, three quarter, or profile

A three quarter turn is the angle I ask for first, because it shows the planes of the face. Dead straight on with a flash is the hardest thing you can hand me, since a flat light on a flat angle gives me no structure to read at all.

AngleWhat it gives meMy call
Three quarter turnThe nose has a shape, the cheek has a plane, the jaw reads as a jawWhat I ask for first
Slight turn, near straight onStrong likeness as long as the light has a directionWorks well
Straight on with direct flashFlat planes, blown highlights, mask-likeSend me another one
Full profileA striking graphic shape, but people often do not recognize someone they loved from a profileGood design, weak likeness
Camera above, chin down (the selfie angle)Enlarged forehead, shrunken chin, distorted proportionsI will not work from it
Camera very close to the faceThe lens pushes the nose forward and shrinks the earsStep back and zoom in instead
[[IMG:tattoo-crying-woman-with-loyalty-script|A tilted face with one direction of light. That is why the cheek and the jaw read as a real face instead of a flat drawing.]]

What I send back

These get an honest no from me every time, and now you know before you ask. None of them are fixable on my end.

  • A screenshot of a screenshot. Every save re-encodes the image and bakes in square artifacts. I cannot tell an artifact from skin texture, so I would end up tattooing the artifacts.
  • A photo of a phone screen or a TV. You get glare, a grid pattern and none of the original detail.
  • A framed print shot through the glass, with the window and your own reflection sitting across your father's face.
  • Anything pulled out of an Instagram or Facebook post. The platform already threw most of that file away before you ever saw it.
  • Beautify and skin smoothing filters. They delete the exact texture that makes a face read as a living person, and most of them quietly reshape the jaw and enlarge the eyes. Family will feel it is off and never be able to say why.
  • App black and white conversions. Send me the color original. That conversion is my decision, and I make it differently for skin than an app makes it for a feed.
  • Anything with the face covered. Sunglasses, a hat brim throwing shade over the eyes, a hand across the mouth, hair across the cheek.
  • A photo of somebody else's tattoo of the same photo. That is a copy of a copy, and it will show.

The hardest case: one old photo of someone who is gone

This is the portrait request I get most often and the hardest one on the table. Somebody has died, there is one photo, it is small, it is from 1979, and it lived in a wallet or sat in a sunny window for thirty years. Most memorial work starts right here.

Here is what actually helps.

  1. Find the physical print. Take it out of the frame. Never shoot it through glass.
  2. Copy it properly. Lay it flat near a window in daylight, no flash, phone held parallel to the print and directly above it, filling the frame with the photo. A flatbed scan at a high setting is stronger still. What ruins it is a tilted phone shot with the shadow of your own head across the corner.
  3. Bring every other photo of him you can find, including the bad ones. The main photo carries the likeness. The extras tell me the truth about the face: how the eyes sat, how wide the bridge of the nose really was, which way the smile went. Ten poor photos plus one decent one is a far stronger hand than one decent photo alone.
  4. Bring somebody who knew him. A brother saying "his smile went up on the left" has rescued more portraits than any piece of software ever will.

About the restore-and-upscale apps: I understand why people run the old photo through one, and I will look at what it gave you. I will not build the likeness from it. Those tools invent. That smooth young face it handed back is an average of a million other faces wearing your father's haircut, and the person who raised you will catch it in about a second without being able to name what changed. I would rather work from an honest grainy original than from a confident stranger.

And I will tell you straight when a photo cannot support a tight realistic portrait. Sometimes the honest answer is a different design: the figure smaller with the detail carried by the composition around it, a pair of hands, a date, a strong graphic piece. Those still read as him. A guessed face does not.

How to send the file without wrecking it

Send the original file, not a copy of a copy. Messaging apps recompress images to keep them small, and a screenshot only captures whatever your screen was showing, which is a fraction of what the file holds.

  • Email the original, or on an iPhone use Mail at Actual Size, or AirDrop it.
  • A Google Drive link works and keeps the full file intact.
  • Instagram DM (@tat2nestuhh) is fine for starting the conversation. Before I draw, I will ask you for the file another way.
  • Do not crop it, do not brighten it, do not convert it. Send it as it is.
  • Send the whole set and tell me which one looks the most like them to you. That one sentence tells me more than you think.

Your camera roll checklist for tonight

Go through your photos with this list and you will know what you have before you contact me. Ten checks, two minutes each.

  1. The face takes up a real portion of the frame, not a corner of a group shot.
  2. Zoomed all the way in on one eye, the lashes and the edge of the iris stay crisp.
  3. The light comes from one direction. There is a bright side and a shadow side.
  4. There is still detail in the shadows, and the forehead and nose are not burned to blank white.
  5. Nothing covers the face. No sunglasses, no hat shadow over the eyes, no hand, no hair across the cheek.
  6. No beautify or skin smoothing filter, and no app black and white conversion.
  7. It is not a screenshot, not a photo of a screen, not a save from a social post.
  8. The head is turned slightly rather than shot dead straight on with a flash.
  9. It is the original file, not one that has passed through five apps.
  10. It looks like how you remember them. Trust that instinct. It is usually right.

Clear all ten and we are in business. Clear eight and send it anyway, and I will tell you exactly what is missing and whether it matters.

Bring me the photo before anything else

Bring your options into the shop or send them ahead, and we will go through them together. I will tell you what that image can hold, how large the piece has to be to hold it, and where on the body it should sit. Portraits are not small tattoos. Detail needs room, and a face squeezed down too small closes up into a smudge with a haircut. You can see the scale I work at in the gallery.

Everything runs on a deposit and a date, which I lay out in how to book with me, and the hourly rate and deposit are on the pricing page. When you have the photo, book a consult. Anointed Ink, 5920 W 111th St, Chicago Ridge, Monday through Saturday, 12pm to 7pm, or call (708) 770-2754.

Don't be average. Be set apart. Start with the right photo.

faq.a: Sometimes, and it is the most common request I get for memorial work. Bring the physical print out of its frame, copy it flat in daylight with no flash, and bring every other photo of that person you can find so I can understand the structure of the face.

faq.q: Should I run the old photo through an AI restore or upscale app first?
faq.a: No. Those tools invent detail, so the smooth face they hand back is an average of other faces wearing your relative's haircut. I will glance at one, but I build the likeness from the original, grain and all.

faq.a: No. A screenshot only captures what your screen was showing and re-encodes the image, which bakes in square artifacts I cannot tell apart from skin texture. Send the original file by email, AirDrop or a Google Drive link.

faq.q: Does a beautify filter really matter on a reference photo?
faq.a: Yes. Skin smoothing deletes the exact texture that makes a face read as a living person, and most filters quietly reshape the jaw and enlarge the eyes. Family will feel the portrait is off without ever being able to say why.

html:
Black and grey lasts longer. That's the straight answer, and I'll give it to you even though I make my living on both. Black ink is carbon, carbon does not change color, and most colored pigments are more complicated molecules that light works against over the years.

That's only half of it though. Plenty of pieces come out weaker in black and grey, and I'll tell you so at the consultation instead of talking you into my favorite lane. What holds up isn't only a pigment question. It's a design question, and the design decides more than the bottle does.

Why black holds its tone

Black holds because of what it's made of. The black in my machine is carbon ground fine and carried in a liquid, and carbon is an element. There's nothing in it for light to take apart into something else, so black stays black.

What changes is intensity, not identity. A black and grey piece at ten years reads softer than it did at ten weeks, but it doesn't read like a different tattoo. If you've seen very old black work with a blue or green cast to it, part of that is what was in bottles forty years ago, and part of it is how any black looks through skin once it thins out over the decades.

The second reason has nothing to do with chemistry. Black and grey is built out of the difference between black, gray, and the open space I deliberately leave alone. When the whole piece softens a fraction, every one of those relationships softens together and stays in the same order. A face still reads as that face. That's why portraits are the subject I argue hardest about.

[[IMG:tattoo-jesus-portrait-with-thorns|Every bit of this is tone. Black, gray, and the open space I left alone. That structure is what gives it the strongest chance of still reading clearly decades from now.]]

Which colors shift, and which ones hold

Color shifts because a colored pigment is a molecule doing a job, and light slowly works against it. But treating "color" as one thing is lazy, because some pigments hold far longer than others and you should know which is which before you pick a palette.

  • Blues and greens in the phthalocyanine family are among the more light-stable pigments made anywhere. The same family shows up in car finishes and printing ink. I'm comfortable running these across large areas.
  • Reds sit in the middle. A deep red keeps reading as red even once it loses punch, which is what matters. A bright hot red has further to fall before it stops looking like the color you asked for.
  • Yellows and oranges are usually the first real color to lose intensity. I use them as accents and I don't let them carry the structure of a piece.
  • White and pastels go first, every time. A pastel is a color cut with white, so it inherits white's weakness. Those bright white hits that make a color piece pop are the part I plan around, not the part I lean on.

Sun exposure speeds all of that up, and it is far harder on color than on carbon. A color sleeve riding a forearm in an open truck window all summer is on a different clock than the same color work on a ribcage. Worth hearing before you commit to full color.

Black and grey vs color, head to head

Here's the comparison the way I'd give it to you across the counter. Neither column wins. They answer different questions.

Black and greyColor
What the pigment isCarbon, an elementPigment molecules, mostly organic
How it reads in ten yearsSofter, same pictureSofter, and some hues have drifted
What carries the imageContrast and valueHue, plus whatever contrast you built in
Time in the chairFewer passesMore passes, usually more sessions
Cost at the same sizeLower, it's fewer hoursHigher, it's more hours
Subjects it suitsFaces, statuary, drapery, lettering, smoke, cloudsFeather work, big cats, florals, anime

What I put in black and grey

Portraits, religious work, lettering, and most memorials go in black and grey. All four are built on tone rather than hue, so color would sit on top as decoration instead of doing the work.

A face is light and shadow. Add color to a portrait and you have made the piece lean on a pigment that drifts while the tonal structure underneath it doesn't. Religious pieces are the same story: statuary, drapery, rays of light, and hands are tonal subjects, and a lot of the reference behind them is carved stone and drawings. Memorials I push toward black and grey for a plainer reason. A memorial has to keep reading clearly for decades, and carbon is the strongest bet for that.

Black and grey Chicano realism is my signature, and its whole language came out of limits. It came up in California in the 1970s, out of prison work where one ink and a fine needle were what you had, and it moved into East LA shops from there. Artists learned to pull an enormous range out of black thinned down into grays. That's why the style holds up. It never depended on anything but black. I go deeper on it in the Chicano style guide.

What genuinely wants color

Aztec feather work, big cats, florals, and anime want color, and I'll say so even when the client walked in asking for black and grey. In those subjects the hue isn't decoration, it's the information.

Take Aztec and cultural work. A warrior's headdress is quetzal feather green, and the mosaic work that tradition is known for is turquoise. Strip the color out and you've drawn the shape of the thing without saying what it was. Here's the honest exception in the same breath: the Sun Stone was carved out of basalt, and although it was once painted, the bare gray stone is how everyone knows it, so a sun stone medallion reads completely right in gray.

[[IMG:tattoo-aztec-warrior-bear|The headdress is the reason this one is in color. Quetzal green and turquoise aren't decoration here, they're the subject.]]

Big cats, wolves, and fish are the other clear case. An amber eye or the orange of a tiger is doing identification work that gray can't do, and color realism earns its extra hours when an animal's color is the point of the animal. Anime is simpler still. It was drawn in color, the reference is in color, and a gray version is a version of somebody else's design they didn't draw.

The middle path I use most

Plenty of my work is neither one nor the other. It's a black and grey composition with one element carrying all the color, and it's what I steer people toward more than any other option.

It works for three reasons. The color has somewhere to be the loudest thing in the frame instead of competing with four other loud things. The gray around it makes a small amount of color hit far harder than a fully saturated piece does. And if that element loses intensity over the years, the composition is still built to stand, because everything holding it up is carbon.

In practice that's a tiger in black and grey with the blossoms in pink. A gray sleeve with one red rose in it. A memorial where the only color in the whole piece is a jersey or a flag. Eyes left their real color inside an otherwise gray portrait.

[[IMG:tattoo-tiger-with-cherry-blossoms|The tiger is black and grey except for the eyes. The eyes, the blossoms, and the butterfly carry all of the color, and that's the whole trick.]]

What color costs you

Color costs more because it takes more hours, not because the ink is expensive. Packing saturated color takes more passes over the same area than laying gray does, so a large color piece usually needs more sessions than a black and grey piece of the same size. My rate is $150 an hour, a deposit books the date, and a full color half sleeve is a multi-session commitment. I would rather you hear that at the counter than find out at session three. I break down how I price work in the piece on prices around the south suburbs.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither one comes cheap. I'm not the artist for bargain hunters.

How to decide on yours

Ask yourself three questions and the answer usually picks itself. I will walk through them with you anyway, but you will get more out of a consultation having thought about them first.

  1. Is this subject about tone or about hue? A face, a statue, praying hands, and a piece of script are tone. A quetzal headdress, a tiger, and a sunflower are hue.
  2. Does the color mean something specific? A team's colors, a flag, the green in the feather work, the exact brown of somebody's eyes. If the color carries meaning, it earns the hours.
  3. Where is it going? A forearm and a ribcage are on different clocks for how long saturated color keeps its punch.

Bring me your reference, your placement, and your budget, and I'll tell you what I'd do with it, including when the answer is that your idea won't work the way you're picturing it. You can book a consultation here or call the shop at (708) 770-2754. We're at 5920 W 111th St in Chicago Ridge, Monday through Saturday, 12pm to 7pm.

html:
The shop rate here is $150 an hour. That is what large and ongoing work is billed at. Small pieces are quoted as one flat price with a shop minimum instead of by the clock, and every booking takes a deposit that comes off the total.

That is the entire price structure. Many shops in the south suburbs do not publish their rates, which is why people spend three evenings messaging shops and still have no idea what anything costs. So here is mine, plainly, along with what actually moves the figure up or down.

The three ways a tattoo gets priced

There are two ways to price a tattoo and one thing that sits on top of both. Large or multi-session work is billed hourly. Small single-session work is quoted as a flat price with a shop minimum. The deposit applies either way and is subtracted from what you owe at the end.

How it is priced When I use it What you pay
Hourly Sleeves, back pieces, portraits, cover-ups, anything running past one sitting $150 per hour of chair time
Flat piece price Small work that starts and finishes in one sitting One figure quoted before you book, with a shop minimum
Deposit Every booking, both of the above Comes off the total. Never added to it

The reason small work gets a flat price is arithmetic, not attitude. A two inch piece takes almost as long to set up, draw, stencil and break down as a six inch piece takes. Billing a twenty minute tattoo by the hour would either cheat you or cheat me, so it gets a price instead of a clock.

What the $150 an hour actually covers

It covers the whole job, not the minutes the machine is running. Most of the work on a custom piece happens before you sit down.

  • The consult, where we figure out whether your idea works on the body part you picked.
  • Drawing the piece for you specifically. Nothing here comes off a wall.
  • Stencil, placement and re-placement until it sits right on your anatomy.
  • Station setup and breakdown, which is not optional and is not free.
  • Written instructions handed to you in person before you leave. That is part of the sitting, not an add-on, and Illinois requires it be done in person on paper rather than off a web page.

I do not bill the drawing separately. It is inside the rate and inside the deposit. What that means for you is that the hours you are charged for are hours you spent in the chair.

What actually moves the price

Five things change the figure, and one thing people expect to change it does not. The subject matter is barely a factor. Two tattoos of the same rose can be an hour apart depending on where they go and how much detail sits inside each square inch.

  • Size. The obvious one, and the one people underestimate. Measure the spot on your own arm with a tape before you guess.
  • Placement. Ribs, sternum, hands, feet, the inside of the arm and the back of the knee are slower work than a flat outer forearm. The skin moves differently there and so do you.
  • Detail density. A portrait and a piece of ornamental blackwork can be identical in size and an hour or two apart in time, because one of them has a human face in it and faces are unforgiving.
  • Color versus black and grey. Color realism has to be packed properly to read the way the reference does, so the same area usually runs longer than the black and grey Chicano realism version of the same design. The hourly rate does not change. The hours do.
  • Fresh skin or a cover-up. Covering old ink means driving more ink into the same space and designing around something that is already there, so cover-ups take longer than a fresh piece of the same size. Always.
  • How many sittings. Two four hour sittings cost what eight hours cost. Nobody gets a discount for splitting it up, and nobody gets punished for it either.
[[IMG:tattoo-tiger-with-cherry-blossoms|The tiger itself is black and grey. The color is in the blossoms, the butterfly and the eyes, and color is not one pass: those blends get packed until they hold, and that packing is the extra time color adds.]]

Why I will not quote from a description alone

Because a description does not contain the two things that set the price: how big it is and where it goes. "A rose on my arm" and "a rose on my ribs" are not the same tattoo and are not the same money.

Send me four things and you get a real figure back instead of a range:

  1. A reference image, or two or three. Screenshots are fine. They do not have to be tattoos.
  2. The placement, with a photo of the actual spot taken in daylight. Your arm, not a diagram.
  3. A rough size in inches. Hold a tape against yourself and tell me the honest measurement.
  4. Black and grey or color.

For a cover-up, add a clear daylight photo of what is already on you, no filter and no flash. I can usually tell you inside a day whether it works, what it would have to become, and whether it needs fading first. The long version of that conversation is in can any tattoo be covered up.

Large work is sold by the sitting, not by the piece

You get the session count before you book, not after. That is what people are really asking when they ask what a sleeve costs, and it is a fair question to expect a straight answer to.

A sleeve is not a purchase, it is a project. We agree on the design, I tell you roughly how many sittings it takes at the length you can actually sit for, and you book them out. Each sitting is billed at the hourly rate. The deposit comes off the last one. If we finish faster than I estimated, you pay for the hours you sat, not the hours I guessed.

People pay for large work the same way they pay for anything else that takes months. A sitting at a time, spaced out, on a schedule that fits their money. I would rather build a good sleeve over eight months than rush a mediocre one into three.

[[IMG:tattoo-norse-wolf-and-longship-sleeve|A sleeve like this is a run of booked sittings, not a single price. You know the count before the first one.]]

The cheapest quote around here is usually the most expensive tattoo you will ever own

This is the part I want you to actually read. A tattoo you regret does not stay at the price you paid for it, because the fix costs more than the original did and the original is already gone.

Run the arithmetic on a bargain piece that goes wrong. You pay for the first tattoo. Then you pay for laser sessions to fade it, spread over months, which is money spent before a needle ever touches you again. Then you pay for a cover-up that has to be larger and darker than the tattoo you actually wanted, because it is now solving a problem instead of being a design. Three bills, months of waiting, and you live with your second choice. I wrote about when fading is worth it in laser fading before a cover-up.

Cheap ink also fails in ways you do not see for a year or two. Lines spread faster than they should. Black packed too heavy goes patchy. Gray wash that was rushed drops out and leaves the piece flat. I see all three of those in my chair, and they usually arrive attached to a story about a deal somebody got.

So when a shop quotes you a fraction of what everyone else quotes, treat it as information. Ask how many hours that number assumes.

[[IMG:tattoo-crowned-skull-cover-up|The stencil over the old tattoo next to the finished piece. A cover-up has to be bigger and darker than what you would have picked on clean skin. That is part of the real cost of a first tattoo you end up covering.]]

Deposits, dates and what I expect from you

A deposit holds your date and comes off your total. It is not a booking fee, it is not extra, and it is not a way to collect money twice. It pays for the drawing that happens before you show up, which is work whether you sit or not.

Give me real notice if you need to move a date and the deposit moves with it. Cancel the morning of or do not show, and the deposit stays with me, because the drawing was already done and the chair sat empty. The current rates live on the pricing page.

Two other things to know before you ask for a figure. You have to be 18, no exceptions, and Illinois law does not allow a parent to consent on your behalf, so bring a government-issued photo ID. And come in fed and rested for a long sitting, because somebody who taps out at hour two has paid for two hours and still leaves with an unfinished piece and another date to book.

What to do with all of this

Decide what you want, measure the spot, and send it in. Look through the gallery first and pull out two or three pieces that are close to the thing in your head, because showing me is faster than describing it.

I have been doing this a long time and I will tell you when an idea does not work at the size or the placement you picked. That conversation is free and it happens before you pay anything. When you are ready, send your idea or call the shop at (708) 770-2754, Monday through Saturday, noon to seven.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.

title: Tattoo Prices in Chicago's South Suburbs, Explained

html:
Booking with me is four steps. You send the idea, I send back a price and a session count, you leave a deposit to hold the date, and you come in with your ID. Nothing gets booked before you know what it costs.

Most of the questions I get are about the deposit, so here is that one up front. It is not a booking fee. It pays for the drawing I do before you sit down, and it comes off your final price.

How to reach me

Three ways, and all three come straight to me. Call or text the shop at (708) 770-2754, send a DM to @tat2nestuhh on Instagram, or message the shop on Facebook.

Text is fastest. I tattoo Monday through Saturday, noon to 7pm, so if the phone rings while I have a machine in my hand I am not answering it. A text waits for me.

What to put in the first message

Six things. Send all six and you get a price back in one reply instead of a week of back and forth.

  • The idea. A sentence or two plus a reference image or two. Not forty saved posts. Two.
  • Placement. Which part of the body, and which side. "Right outer forearm" is an answer. "Arm" is not.
  • Rough size in inches. Put a tape measure on the spot and give me the number. "Medium" is not a size, and size moves a quote more than anything else.
  • Black and grey, or color. If you are not sure, say so and I will tell you which one the design actually wants.
  • Whether it is a cover-up. If it is, send a clear daylight photo of the existing tattoo, shot flat on, no flash, no filter.
  • Your real availability. Weekdays or Saturdays, and any weeks you are out. The honest version, not the one where you are free whenever.

Here is the difference that makes.

What I usually getWhat gets you a number back
"How much for a sleeve?""Full sleeve, left arm, black and grey, Aztec theme, Saturdays free starting in November."
"Small one on my wrist, how much?""One word in script, inner wrist, about 3 inches across, black and grey."
"Can you cover this up?" with no photo"Cover-up over an old name, right forearm, roughly 4 by 2 inches, daylight photo attached, open on the design."

If you are sending me a face, the reference photo is the whole job. A screenshot of a screenshot will not carry into skin, so I will ask you for the original file. More on that in how to pick the reference photo for a portrait.

What happens next: a straight quote and a session count

You get a real number and the number of sittings it takes, before anything is booked. Not a range, and not "we will see when you get here."

Large and ongoing work runs at the shop rate of $150 an hour. Small pieces get quoted flat, because a two inch tattoo takes far more setup than it takes needle time. If your piece needs three sittings, you hear "three sittings" now, not on the day of the second one. What moves the number is broken down on the pricing and deposits page, and at more length in what tattoos cost around here.

You will also hear the other answer. If the design will not hold at the size you want, or the placement will close that detail up over the years, I say so in the same message. Sometimes that means a bigger piece, sometimes a different design, and sometimes it means I am not the right artist for it.

Quality takes time. Excellence takes experience. And neither comes cheap. I am not the artist for bargain hunters.
[[IMG:tattoo-dragon-back-piece|A back piece is not a sitting. You get the session count before you commit, not halfway through.]]

Why there is a deposit

The deposit exists because the work starts before you do. Every piece here is drawn for one person, at one size, for one spot on one body, and that drawing happens on my time in the days before your appointment.

It comes off the final price. It is never added on top. On a multi-session piece it comes off the last sitting.

The other half of it is the date. When I hold an afternoon for you, that afternoon is gone for everybody else. If you cancel the morning of, the drawing is already done and it fits nobody but you, so the deposit stays with the work. Give me real notice and your deposit moves to the new date without an argument.

[[IMG:tattoo-crowned-skull-cover-up|The stencil over the old tattoo, next to the finished piece. That stencil is what a deposit pays for.]]

The amount scales with the piece. A two hour session and a six sitting back piece are not the same commitment, so ask when you get your quote and you will get a straight number.

Bring a government-issued photo ID, every visit

Bring a driver's license, a state ID or a passport: something issued by a government, carrying both your photograph and your date of birth. That is exactly how Illinois requires age to be verified (77 Ill. Adm. Code 797.400(k)).

I check it every visit. That includes people I have tattooed ten times. The rule attaches to the procedure, not to whether I recognize your face, so nobody gets waved through and nobody should take it personally.

A picture of your ID on your phone does not count. Neither does a school ID.

18 and over, no exceptions

You have to be 18 or older to get tattooed here. There are no exceptions, and Illinois law does not allow a parent to consent on your behalf.

That is not shop attitude, it is 720 ILCS 5/12C-35. The statute makes it a Class A misdemeanor to tattoo, or even to offer to tattoo, anyone under 18, and it contains no clause for a parent to sign around it. There is nothing here for me to bend.

The same statute covers the room itself. Anyone under 18 has to be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian to be on the premises while tattooing is going on. So if you are the one in the chair and your kid would otherwise be on their own, arrange childcare first.

If you are not 18 yet, hold on to the idea and the reference. They will keep until you are.

Picking a date and showing up

The shop is open Monday through Saturday, noon to 7pm, closed Sunday. Small work books sooner than large work and Saturdays go first, so tell me up front if Saturday is your only day.

Eat a real meal before you come, not a coffee. Wear something that gives clean access to the placement, and plan for the session to run the full length you were quoted rather than the length you hoped for.

What comes after the session is handled in person. Illinois requires the instructions for that to be given to you out loud and in writing, specific to the work you just got, so I go over them with you at the counter before you leave. A web page cannot do that job and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

That is the whole process. Look through the gallery and decide whether my hand is right for your idea, particularly if you are after black and grey Chicano realism, a portrait or a memorial. Then send me the six things and let us get a number on it. Start here.

faq.a: No. The deposit comes off the final price and is never added to it. It pays for the drawing that happens before you sit down, and on a multi-session piece it comes off the last sitting.

faq.q: What should I put in my first message to book?
faq.a: Six things: the idea with one or two reference images, the placement and which side, a rough size in inches, whether you want black and grey or color, whether it is a cover-up (with a daylight photo of the existing tattoo), and your real availability. Send all six and you get a price back in one reply.

faq.q: Do I get a price before anything is booked?
faq.a: Yes. You get a real number and the number of sittings it takes before any date is held. Large and ongoing work runs at $150 an hour and small pieces are quoted flat.

faq.q: Do I need to bring ID if Nestor has tattooed me before?
faq.a: Yes, every visit. Illinois requires age to be verified with government-issued identification carrying both a photograph and a date of birth, so a driver's license, state ID or passport gets checked each time, including for repeat clients.

faq.q: Can a parent consent to a tattoo for someone under 18 in Illinois?
faq.a: No. Illinois law has no parental consent exception, and 720 ILCS 5/12C-35 makes it a Class A misdemeanor to tattoo or even offer to tattoo anyone under 18. The same statute also requires anyone under 18 to be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian just to be on the premises while tattooing is going on.

title: How to Book a Tattoo With Me: Deposits and Dates

html:
The question I get every spring is when to get a tattoo before vacation, and the answer is the same for a trip, a wedding or a graduation. Start from the date you want to be showing the piece and count backward. That is the whole method. Most people count forward from today, which is how somebody ends up asking for a half sleeve four weeks before a wedding.

Here are the lead times I plan around in Chicago Ridge, and the months that tend to be open.

Count backward from the event, not forward from today

Three dates matter, and most people bring me only one. There is the event date, the date the last session has to be done, and the date you put a deposit down.

The gap between the last two is what people skip. Say a wedding is June 14 and you want a forearm piece finished for it. The job is not "book something in June." The job is: last session in mid May, first session in April, which means you are calling me in March.

So give me the event date up front. I will do that math with you before you pay anything, and if it does not work I will say so instead of taking a deposit and hoping.

How far ahead to book, by size

Small pieces need weeks. Large pieces need months. This is what it looks like in practice at my shop.

PieceTime in the chairBook this far ahead
A date, a name, a palm-size piece of script1 to 2 hours2 to 3 weeks
One forearm piece or a single portrait4 to 6 hours, one or two sittings4 to 6 weeks
Half sleeve3 to 4 sittings3 to 4 months
Full sleeve5 to 7 sittings6 to 9 months
Back piece or full chest8 or more sittings9 to 12 months
Cover-up, any sizeConsult before anything gets bookedAdd 4 weeks, or several months if I want it faded first

Those count back from the day you need the last session done, and on multi-session work they include the sittings, not just the wait to get onto my calendar. A back piece is a year of your life, on and off, and it should be treated that way from the first call.

[[IMG:tattoo-blackletter-year-2001|A year in blackletter. One sitting, and I can usually fit something like this inside a few weeks.]]

Multi-session work gets its dates locked as a block

If a piece takes more than two sittings, we book every session at once, on the day the deposit is paid. I do not book session one and figure out the rest later.

The reason is arithmetic. I space sessions three to four weeks apart, so a full sleeve at six sessions is fifteen to twenty weeks from the first sitting to the last, before you add the wait to start. Book them one at a time and every next date gets whatever is left after the people who planned. A five month sleeve quietly becomes a ten month sleeve.

Booked as a block you can usually keep the same weekday and start time each round, and you get the session count before you commit instead of three sittings in.

[[IMG:tattoo-norse-wolf-and-longship-sleeve|A sleeve is not an appointment. It is a block of dates I set before we start.]]

Planning a sleeve around a wedding or a vacation

For a hard date, I want the last session finished with weeks to spare, not the week of. Build a buffer into the plan and treat it as part of the schedule, not as slack you can spend.

Two weeks of buffer on a single-session piece. Four to six weeks on anything multi-session. That covers what actually happens: you get sent out of state for work, I lose a day, a session runs long and we need one more date to finish it right.

Send the placement in that first message too. Placement drives the session count and the session count drives how early you start, so a wrist piece and a rib piece the same size are not the same booking. If you are still deciding, go through the gallery and come to me with a direction. A week matters when you are counting backward.

Which months fill and which months are quiet

January through early March is usually the quietest stretch of my year. May and June are the hardest months to get into, and it is not close.

Graduations stack up through May. Weddings run May into October, vacation season takes June through August, and pool season pulls a wave of bookings right before it starts. December fills early with holiday work, then the calendar goes flat in January.

If your date is flexible, book in winter. More choice of days, longer sittings, a real shot at the exact dates you want on a big piece. If you want a sleeve of black and grey Chicano realism ready for next summer, call in the fall so the sittings start in the quiet months. Not May.

[[IMG:tattoo-dragon-back-piece|Back pieces get started in winter. The people who plan them early are the people who finish.]]

Booking around your training week

Look at your week, find the day you already do the least, and put the appointment there. My hours are noon to 7pm, Monday through Saturday, and I am closed Sunday.

Six hours is the longest I book in one day, and a sitting that size takes the afternoon and the evening with it. If you train early, a noon start costs you nothing. If you train after work, that sitting and your workout want the same block of the day, so move the appointment to another weekday instead of cramming both in and showing up late to mine.

If you are training toward a date of your own, say so when you book. I would rather place the sessions around your calendar at the start than move five appointments in April.

Cover-ups need extra runway

A cover-up does not book on the same timeline as fresh work. Add a consult first, and if I ask for laser fading, add months to the calendar rather than weeks.

So send a clear daylight photo of what is already there in your first message. I will tell you whether it can be covered at the size you want and whether I want it faded, and that answer is often the difference between making your date and missing it. I explain when I ask for fading, and why, in the post on laser fading before a cover-up.

The deposit is what holds the date, not the conversation

Until a deposit is paid, your date is open to whoever books it next. A text thread does not hold a day on my calendar, and people lose June Saturdays over three days of thinking it over.

The shop rate is $150 an hour for large and ongoing work, small pieces are quoted flat, and the deposit comes off the total, never on top of it. Give me reasonable notice and it moves with you. No-show and it stays, because the drawing was already done. Detail is on the pricing and deposits page and in how to book a tattoo with me.

What to send me when you book

  • The event date and what it is. Wedding, graduation, trip, reunion.
  • Placement and a rough size in inches.
  • Reference images, including anything you saved from the gallery.
  • If it is a cover-up, a clear daylight photo of the existing piece.
  • Your real availability. The weekdays you can genuinely sit for six hours, not the ones you wish you could.

Text or call (708) 770-2754, or start on the booking page. If your date is too tight for what you are asking for, I will tell you in the first message rather than the fourth. Quality takes time, and the calendar is part of the time.
